Grade 5 · Unit 5.4

Earth's Spheres, Water, and Communities

How do Earth’s spheres interact, where is Earth’s water, and how do communities protect it?

Concept 1

Spheres interact

A rainstorm is the atmosphere and hydrosphere eroding the geosphere while the biosphere’s roots hold soil.

Diagram

Spheres

geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere labels.

“Rock, water, air, and life all connect.”

Try it

Stream model

sloped tray with water channel.

“Make a tiny river. Watch it cut a channel.”

You did this before / what is new: You tested erosion in 4.5; now you label the four Earth spheres.

Data

Stream-tray results

table: no plants 12 spoonfuls of sediment moved; grass 4 spoonfuls; stones 7 spoonfuls.

“Plants helped hold soil. Water still moved sediment.”

Real world

Michigan hill after rain

rain moving soil down a hill and grass roots in soil.

“Rain moves soil. Roots help.”

Concept 2

Most Earth water is salty, and much fresh water is frozen

Earth has limited liquid fresh water; most water is salt, and much fresh water is ice.

Try it

Graph the water

100 small squares.

“Color 97 squares salty ocean. Color 2 squares frozen fresh water. Color 1 square for fresh water under the ground. Lakes and rivers are less than one square: draw a tiny dot.”

Data

Provided percentages

about 97% salt water, about 3% fresh water. Of the fresh water, most is ice and most of the rest is underground; lakes and rivers are only a tiny part.

“Most Earth water is salty. Most fresh water is ice or underground. Lakes and rivers hold very little.”

Diagram

Student-made bar graph

bars for salt water, frozen fresh water, fresh water underground, and lakes and rivers.

“Our graph shows the fresh water we can easily use, in lakes and rivers, is a very small part.”

Real world

Great Lakes

Great Lakes map.

“The Great Lakes hold lots of fresh water, but Earth still has mostly salty ocean.”

Concept 3

Communities use science to protect resources

Communities use information and design to protect water, land, and air; science helps choose solutions.

Real world

Case cards

three cards: city rain-garden program, dune-grass restoration, farm fertilizer rules.

“Each card shows a problem, a solution, and how science helped.”

Try it

Combine information

chart with columns: Problem, Solution, Evidence, Who helped.

“Put the clues together. How did science help?”

Data

Rain-garden runoff

table: parking lot runoff 10 buckets; rain garden runoff 6 buckets; water looks cleaner.

“The rain garden slowed and cleaned runoff.”

Real world

Sleeping Bear Dunes

dune grass blowing in wind.

“Grass roots hold sand. People plant it to protect dunes.”

Hands-on · Design or investigate

Try it at home or in class

Design and test a model solution to protect a slope or shoreline. Compare two solutions, such as grass, stones, or a foil barrier. Criteria: less sediment moved. Constraints: same amount of water each test, limited materials, 10 minutes.

Try it

What you need

shallow tray, soil/sand, water, cardboard, foil, tape, craft sticks, small pebbles, paper cups, graph paper, colored pencils, index cards.

Safety: wash hands after soil/sand trays; do not drink the water; clean spills right away; adult handles any warm water if used.

Try it

What you do

build a model slope or shore; test how plants, stones, or barriers change sediment movement; graph Earth’s water; make community case-card summaries. You did this before / what is new: You graphed data in 5.2; now you graph Earth’s water yourself.

No time or no good weather? Use this data

This data is a backup. It lets you practice reading evidence, but the standard expects you to collect your own when you can.

Check yourself

What did you learn?

0 of 4 correct

Words to know

geosphere
Earth’s rock and soil.
hydrosphere
Earth’s water.
atmosphere
Earth’s air.
biosphere
Earth’s living things.
erosion
moving of rock/soil pieces.
sediment
small pieces of rock or soil moved by water, wind, or ice.
resource
material people can use.
runoff
water that flows over land instead of soaking in.
trade-off
giving up one thing to get another.
community
people living and working together in a place.
Tutor notes: misconceptions, standards, pacing

Pacing: five 30-minute sessions.

Common misconceptions to listen for:

  • “Earth has plenty of liquid fresh water everywhere.” Correct: most water is salty; much fresh water is frozen.
  • “Most fresh water is in rivers and lakes.” Correct: much fresh water is frozen or underground.
  • “The geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, and biosphere stay separate.” Correct: they interact.
  • “Only nonliving things change Earth’s surface.” Correct: living things, like roots and people, also change the surface.
  • “Community solutions cannot reduce harm.” Correct: solutions can reduce harm, but they cannot eliminate all risk.
  • “One solution, like recycling, fixes everything.” Correct: communities need many solutions, and each has trade-offs.
  • “A rain garden stops all flooding forever.” Correct: it reduces runoff; it does not stop all water problems.

Limits and cautions:

  • Water percentages are rounded to 97/2/1 squares; lakes and rivers are under 1% of fresh water, so draw them as a dot.
  • The sphere model is simplified; real Earth interactions happen over many scales.
  • This unit does not teach the full water cycle; Unit 4 does that.
  • This unit does not teach plate tectonics; Unit 5 does that.
  • Community protection examples require obtaining and combining information; the three case cards guarantee access even if students cannot research independently.

Michigan Science Standards this unit earns:

  • 5-ESS2-1: Model interactions of geosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere, and atmosphere.
  • 5-ESS2-2: Analyze data on amounts of Earth’s water and ice.
  • 5-ESS3-1: Obtain information about how communities protect Earth’s resources and environment.

Connections: Builds on: 4.5 Earth’s Surface: Rocks, Maps, Erosion, Resources; 3.2 Weather, Climate, and Hazards; 5.2 Gravity, Stars, and Sky Patterns; K–5 Unit 0: How Science Works. Builds toward: Unit 4 Weather & the Water Cycle; Unit 6 Natural Hazards; Unit 13 Energy Resources & Human Impact; 7.7 Earth Resources & Human Impact.
